claims.evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4A-C showing lack of thymus reconstitution after Fermt3-/- FL cell transfer.

claims.claim: Rag2-/- recipient thymi that received Fermt3-/- FL cells contained almost no DN1-2 cells.
claims.source: The transfer of Fermt3-/- FL cells failed to reconstitute T cell development in the thymus of Rag2-/- recipient mice (Figure 4A–C), which also contained almost no DN1-2 cells (Figure 4D,E).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4D,E showing near absence of DN1-2 cells.

claims.claim: A very small number of Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors entered the Rag2-/- recipient thymus and differentiated into DN4 cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, a very small number of Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors entered the Rag2-/- recipient thymus, differentiated into DN4 cells (Figure 4D,F)
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4D,F showing presence of DN4 cells.

claims.claim: Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors that entered the Rag2-/- recipient thymus produced a small number of circulating CD4 and CD8 T cells, which homed to the spleen.
claims.source: Interestingly, a very small number of Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors entered the Rag2-/- recipient thymus, differentiated into DN4 cells (Figure 4D,F) and produced a small number of circulating CD4 and CD8 T cells, which homed to the spleen of Rag2-/- mice (Figure 4G–K)
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4G-K showing presence of CD4 and CD8 T cells in blood and spleen.

claims.claim: Kindlin-3 is very important for T cell progenitor homing to the adult thymus, but once in the thymus the progenitor cells differentiate into mature SP T cells that are released into the circulation.
claims.source: Interestingly, a very small number of Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors entered the Rag2-/- recipient thymus, differentiated into DN4 cells (Figure 4D,F) and produced a small number of circulating CD4 and CD8 T cells, which homed to the spleen of Rag2-/- mice (Figure 4G–K) indicating that kindlin-3 is very important for T cell progenitor homing to the adult thymus, but once in the thymus the progenitor cells differentiate into mature SP T cells that are released into the circulation.
claims.evidence: Based on inference from the observation that a small number of Fermt3-/- progenitors can complete T cell development once they enter the thymus.

claims.claim: Conditional deletion of Fermt3 by polyIC injection into Fermt3fl/fl/Mx1-Cre mice resulted in almost no DN (Linneg) cells in their thymi.
claims.source: Since kindlin-3-deficient HSCs show an approximately 5-fold reduced homing capacity to the bone marrow, which might eventually impact on T cell progenitor generation (Ruppert et al., 2015), we conditionally deleted Fermt3 by injecting polyIC into Fermt3fl/fl/Mx1-Cre mice and detected almost no DN (Linneg) cells in their thymi, whereas control thymi from polyIC-treated Fermt3fl/fl mice clearly contained a discrete population of DN1-2 stage T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A showing loss of DN cells after conditional deletion.

claims.claim: In mixed FL cell chimeras with 90% Fermt3-/- FL cells and 10% WT FL cells, only around 25% of the DN cells were of CD45.2 (Fermt3-/-) origin.
claims.source: In addition, we generated mixed FL cell chimeras by transferring nine times more Fermt3-/- FL cells than WT FL cells into lethally irradiated recipient mice and compared their homing capacity to the thymus. To discriminate between both cell populations the WT FL cells were isolated from B6.SJL embryos, which express the CD45.1 allelic variant, while the Fermt3-/- embryos are from a C57BL/6 background expressing CD45.2. Despite the excess in transferred kindlin-3-deficient FL cells, only around 25% of the DN cells were of CD45.2 origin.
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B showing disproportionate representation of Fermt3-/- cells.

claims.claim: Chimeras made from 90% WT CD45.2 cells and 10% WT B6.SJL CD45.1 cells showed the 9:1 ratio in DN and all later T cell stages.
claims.source: As a control, chimeras made from 90% WT CD45.2 cells and 10% WT B6.SJL CD45.1 cells showed the 9:1 ratio in DN and all later T cell stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B showing expected ratios in control chimeras.

claims.claim: Only CD45+ leukocytes were EGFP-positive in thymi from Kindlin-3-EGFP knockin mice, while CD31+ endothelial cells and EPCAM+ thymic epithelial cells were EGFP negative.
claims.source: Moreover, to exclude a defect in a non-hematopoietic cell type as cause for the Fermt3-/- T cell progenitor homing defect, we analysed thymi from Kindlin-3-EGFP knockin mice, which express kindlin-3 tagged C-terminally with EGFP. Flow cytometry of their thymi revealed that only CD45+ leukocytes were EGFP-positive and that CD31+ endothelial cells and EPCAM+ thymic epithelial cells were EGFP negative (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 showing cell-type specific kindlin-3 expression.

claims.claim: The homing defect of kindlin-3-deficient T cell progenitors is of hematopoietic origin.
claims.source: Altogether, these experiments show that kindlin-3-deficient T cell progenitors have a strong defect in homing to the postnatal and adult thymus and that the homing defect is of hematopoietic origin.
claims.evidence: Based on inference from multiple experiments including conditional deletion, mixed chimeras, and kindlin-3-EGFP expression analysis.

claims.claim: The first wave of WT CD45+ progenitor cells was observed within the perithymic mesenchyme at E11.5.
claims.source: In line with previous reports (Douagi et al., 2000; Itoi et al., 2001), we observed the first wave of WT CD45+ progenitor cells within the perithymic mesenchyme at E11.5, and initial migration into the thymus primordium at E12.0 and scattering throughout the thymus at E12.5 and E13.5 (Figure 5A–F).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5A-F and citations to previous studies (Douagi et al., 2000; Itoi et al., 2001).

claims.claim: Fermt3-/- progenitor cells could be detected in the thymus primordium and the surrounding mesenchyme, however at lower numbers than WT.
claims.source: Interestingly, also Fermt3-/- progenitor cells could be detected in the thymus primordium and the surrounding mesenchyme, however at lower numbers (Figure 5A–E).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification in Figure 5A-E showing reduced but present Fermt3-/- progenitors.

claims.claim: CD45+ progenitor cells accumulated at E13.5 in the Fermt3-/- thymus and continued developing into DN1-2 cells.
claims.source: Despite the reduction, CD45+ progenitor cells accumulated at E13.5 in the Fermt3-/- thymus (Figure 5D) and continued developing into DN1-2 cells (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry data in Figure 5D,F showing progenitor accumulation and differentiation.

claims.claim: A dramatic drop in the DN1-2 population was observed in Fermt3-/- thymi at E15-16.
claims.source: Strikingly, a dramatic drop in the DN1-2 population was observed in Fermt3-/- thymi at E15-16 (Figure 5G,H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5G,H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B showing reduced DN1-2 cells at later embryonic stages.

claims.claim: The absolute numbers of Linneg, c-kithi, CD45+, PIR+ T cell progenitors were comparable between WT and Fermt3-/- FLs.
claims.source: The flow cytometric analyses revealed that the absolute numbers of Linneg, c-kithi, CD45+, PIR+ T cell progenitors were comparable between WT and Fermt3-/- FLs, while their frequency, due to a decreased cellularity of Fermt3-/- FLs, was increased (Figure 6A–C).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6A-C showing similar absolute numbers of T cell progenitors in FL.

claims.claim: The frequency of T cell progenitors in Fermt3-/- FLs was increased due to decreased cellularity of Fermt3-/- FLs.
claims.source: The flow cytometric analyses revealed that the absolute numbers of Linneg, c-kithi, CD45+, PIR+ T cell progenitors were comparable between WT and Fermt3-/- FLs, while their frequency, due to a decreased cellularity of Fermt3-/- FLs, was increased (Figure 6A–C).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6A-C showing increased frequency of progenitors.

claims.claim: The numbers of circulating WT and Fermt3-/- Linneg, c-kithi, PIR+ T cell progenitors increased between E11.5 to E12.
claims.source: The numbers of circulating WT and Fermt3-/- Linneg, c-kithi, PIR+ T cell progenitors increased between E11.5 to E12.
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6D,E showing increased circulating progenitors at E12.

claims.claim: The frequency of WT T cell progenitors steadily decreased between E12 and E13.5, while T cell progenitors accumulated in the circulation of Fermt3-/- fetuses.
claims.source: However, while the frequency of WT T cell progenitors steadily decreased between E12 and E13.5, the T cell progenitors accumulated in the circulation of Fermt3-/- fetuses due to their reduced extravasation from pharyngeal vessels and/or impaired migration towards the thymus primordium (Figure 6D,E).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6D,E showing differential kinetics of circulating progenitors.

claims.claim: WT as well as Fermt3-/- FL cells moved persistently towards the thymic lobes in the thymus attraction assay.
claims.source: Progenitor migration towards the thymic lobes was monitored for 36 to 48 hr by time-lapse video microscopy, which revealed that WT as well as Fermt3-/- FL cells moved persistently towards the thymic lobes, while migration was not induced when thymic lobes were absent (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data in Figure 7B showing directed migration of both WT and Fermt3-/- cells.

claims.claim: CD45.2+ Fermt3-/- donor cells normally developed into DP, CD4 and CD8 SP cells in fetal thymus organ culture.
claims.source: Consistent with our in vivo data, CD45.2+ Fermt3-/- donor cells normally developed into DP, CD4 and CD8 SP cells (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 7D showing normal T cell development in FTOC.

claims.claim: Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors normally develop in the FL, are released into the circulation, sense the chemokine gradient, leave the pharyngeal vessel, migrate towards the thymus primordium, invade the thymus capsule and differentiate into different T cell subsets.
claims.source: Altogether these findings indicate that Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors normally develop in the FL, are released into the circulation, sense the chemokine gradient, leave the pharyngeal vessel, albeit less efficiently than WT T cell progenitors, migrate towards the thymus primordium, invade the thymus capsule and differentiate into different T cell subsets.
claims.evidence: Based on inference from multiple experimental observations including FL analysis, thymus attraction assay, and FTOC.

claims.claim: The differential efficacy of Fermt3-/- T cell progenitor homing to the avascular and vascularized thymus was not due to different kindlin-3 and talin-1 protein levels in FL-derived and postnatal T progenitor cells.
claims.source: The differential efficacy of Fermt3-/- T cell progenitor homing to the avascular and vascularized thymus was neither due to different kindlin-3 and talin-1 protein levels in lysates from sorted FL-derived T progenitor cells (Linneg, c-kit+, PIR+) isolated from E13.5 embryos and DN1 cells (Linneg, CD44+, CD25-) isolated from P6 thymi nor from an upregulation of talin-1 in Fermt3-/- PIR+ T cell progenitors (Figure 8A,B).
claims.evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 8A,B showing similar protein levels.

claims.claim: Flow cytometry excluded differences in surface expression of α4, αL, β1, β2, β3 and β7 integrins on FL-derived T progenitor cells.
claims.source: Flow cytometry also excluded differences in surface expression of α4, αL, β1, β2, β3 and β7 integrins on FL-derived T progenitor cells (Linneg, c-kit+, PIR+) (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) and BM-derived LSK cells (Ruppert et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and citation to Ruppert et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The CD31-positive vascular network was indistinguishable in E13.5 and E15.5 thymi from WT and Fermt3-/- mice.
claims.source: Similarly, the CD31-positive vascular network was indistinguishable in E13.5 and E15.5 thymi from WT and Fermt3-/- mice excluding the possibility that a potential kindlin-3 expression in endothelial cells (Bialkowska et al., 2010) accounts for the defective homing to the vascularized thymus (data not shown).
claims.evidence: Based on observation of normal vascular networks and citation to Bialkowska et al., 2010.

claims.claim: VCAM-1, ICAM-1 and ICAM-2 expression was lower in pharyngeal vessels compared to intrathymic vessels.
claims.source: Since adhesion and extravasation of Fermt3-/- T cells can occur on inflamed endothelium expressing high levels of VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 (Manevich-Mendelson et al., 2009; Moretti et al., 2013), we determined the expression of VCAM-1, ICAM-1 and ICAM-2 by immunostaining and flow cytometry and found them even lower expressed in pharyngeal vessels compared to intrathymic vessels.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry data in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A-E and citations to Manevich-Mendelson et al., 2009 and Moretti et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Blood flow velocity and shear rates increased in the yolk sac vasculature between E12.5 to E16.5.
claims.source: We therefore hypothesized that Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors show impaired adhesion to the vascular endothelium when blood flow velocity and shear forces increase during intrauterine development. To test this hypothesis, we injected red fluorescent microbeads into the yolk-sac vasculature of E12.5 to E16.5 embryos and measured blood flow velocity by intravital microscopy. We found an increase in blood flow velocity (Figure 8C) and shear rates (Figure 8D) between E12.5 to 16.5.
claims.evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy measurements shown in Figure 8C,D.

claims.claim: Isolated T cell progenitors hardly adhered to P-selectin, CCL21/CCL25 and ICAM-1 in flow chamber assays.
claims.source: Accordingly, in vitro flow chamber assays revealed that isolated T cell progenitors (Linneg, c-kit+, CD45+, Pir+) hardly adhered to P-selectin, CCL21/CCL25 and ICAM-1 (Figure 8E)
claims.evidence: Supported by flow chamber assay data in Figure 8E showing minimal adhesion to ICAM-1.

claims.claim: T cell progenitors readily adhered to P-selectin, CCL21/CCL25 and VCAM-1 in a shear stress-dependent manner.
claims.source: Accordingly, in vitro flow chamber assays revealed that isolated T cell progenitors (Linneg, c-kit+, CD45+, Pir+) hardly adhered to P-selectin, CCL21/CCL25 and ICAM-1 (Figure 8E), while they readily adhered to P-selectin, CCL21/CCL25 and VCAM-1 in a shear stress-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: Supported by flow chamber assay data in Figure 8F showing adhesion to VCAM-1.

claims.claim: Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors adhered to VCAM-1 but displayed a significantly reduced shear force resistance.
claims.source: Interestingly, Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors adhered to VCAM-1 but displayed a significantly reduced shear force resistance (Figure 8F)
claims.evidence: Supported by flow chamber assay data in Figure 8F showing detachment at higher shear rates.

claims.claim: The increase in blood flow velocity and shear forces during fetal development prevents Fermt3-/- T cell progenitor adhesion and extravasation at intrathymic vessels.
claims.source: Interestingly, Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors adhered to VCAM-1 but displayed a significantly reduced shear force resistance (Figure 8F) suggesting that the increase in blood flow velocity and shear forces during fetal development prevents Fermt3-/- T cell progenitor adhesion and extravasation at intrathymic vessels.
claims.evidence: Based on inference from the observation that Fermt3-/- progenitors cannot resist high shear forces and that shear forces increase during development.

claims.claim: A reduced number of adherent Fermt3 hypomorphic T cells was observed in the LN vasculature compared to WT cells.
claims.source: As expected, we observed a reduced number of adherent Fermt3 hypomorphic T cells in the LN vasculature compared to WT cells (Figure 8H,I).
claims.evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy data in Figure 8H,I showing reduced adhesion of hypomorphic cells.

claims.claim: Fermt3 hypomorphic cells adhered preferentially in vessel segments where blood flow velocity and shear rates were lower compared to WT T cells.
claims.source: We then injected fluorescent microspheres and measured the blood flow velocities in LN vessel segments and determined shear rates adherent cells were exposed to in those vessels. We found that Fermt3 hypomorphic cells adhered preferentially in vessel segments where blood flow velocity and shear rates were lower compared to WT T cells. The latter adhered to vessel segments with higher blood flow velocities and shear rates (Figure 8J,K).
claims.evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy measurements in Figure 8J,K showing differential adhesion based on shear rates.

claims.claim: Kindlin-3 is crucial to stabilize integrin-mediated T cell adhesion to vessel walls exposed to high vascular shear forces.
claims.source: These findings indicate that kindlin-3 is crucial to stabilize integrin-mediated T cell adhesion to vessel walls exposed to high vascular shear forces.
claims.evidence: Based on inference from multiple experiments showing that cells with reduced kindlin-3 cannot adhere at high shear rates.

claims.claim: In the absence of kindlin-3, a well-organized thymus with normal thymus architecture consisting of the four major compartments is initially formed.
claims.source: We found that in the absence of kindlin-3 a well-organized thymus with normal thymus architecture consisting of the four major compartments (subcapsular zone, cortex, medulla and cortico-medullary junction) is initially formed.
claims.evidence: Based on histological and immunofluorescence observations of thymic architecture.

claims.claim: Chemokine-driven migration and positioning of developing T cells to specialized thymic microdomains is not impaired in the absence of kindlin-3.
claims.source: The presence and clear separation of DP thymocytes in the cortex from SP CD4 and CD8 T cells in the medulla of postnatal thymi indicate that chemokine-driven migration and positioning of developing T cells to specialized thymic microdomains is not impaired in the absence of kindlin-3 allowing a well-orchestrated developmental maturation from T cell progenitors to mature T cells.
claims.evidence: Based on inference from the observation of normal spatial organization of T cell subsets in Fermt3-/- thymi.

claims.claim: Chemokine sensing and leukocyte migration within a 3D environment can occur in the absence of kindlin-3.
claims.source: Thus, our data indicate that chemokine sensing and leukocyte migration within a 3D environment can occur in the absence of kindlin-3´s role to regulate integrin activity, which is in line with a previous report (Lämmermann et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Based on inference from observations of normal intrathymic migration and citation to Lämmermann et al., 2008.

claims.claim: The thymi from kindlin-3 deficient mice began shrinking after birth.
claims.source: While early thymic development is hardly affected by the lack of kindlin-3, the thymi from kindlin-3 deficient mice began shrinking after birth.
claims.evidence: Based on observations of thymus size and cellularity over time.

claims.claim: Kindlin-3-deficient thymocytes exhibited reduced proliferation rates due to a weakened interaction with thymic APCs.
claims.source: We found two main reasons for the thymic atrophy. First, kindlin-3-deficient thymocytes exhibited reduced proliferation rates due to a weakened interaction with thymic APCs.
claims.evidence: Based on BrdU incorporation assays and in vitro proliferation assays with DCs.

claims.claim: A weakened interaction with APCs was reported for CD4 T cells isolated from LFA-1 and talin-1 knockout mice to cause reduced T cell proliferation.
claims.source: A weakened interaction with APCs was also reported for CD4 T cells isolated from LFA-1 and talin-1 knockout mice to cause reduced T cell proliferation (Graf et al., 2007; Kandula and Abraham, 2004; Wernimont et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Graf et al., 2007; Kandula and Abraham, 2004; Wernimont et al., 2011.

claims.claim: A severe T cell progenitor homing defect becomes apparent at the end of embryogenesis in kindlin-3-deficient mice.
claims.source: Secondly, we observed a severe T cell progenitor homing defect, which becomes apparent at the end of embryogenesis.
claims.evidence: Based on flow cytometry data showing dramatic reduction in DN1-2 cells at E15-16.

claims.claim: FL-derived T cell progenitors start colonizing the thymus anlage at around embryonic day E11.5.
claims.source: FL-derived T cell progenitors start colonizing the thymus anlage at around embryonic day (E) 11.5.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge of T cell development and supported by immunofluorescence observations.

claims.claim: The thymus anlage is initially avascular.
claims.source: Since the thymus anlage is initially avascular, T cell progenitors exit the adjacent pharyngeal vessels, migrate towards the thymic primordium, cross the dense extracellular matrix of the thymic capsule and finally settle in the thymic tissue.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge of thymus development.

claims.claim: Kindlin-3-dependent adhesiveness through multiple integrin classes expressed on T lymphoid progenitors is essential for their homing to the vascularized thymus.
claims.source: This process is critically dependent on kindlin-3. Furthermore, our findings also show that kindlin-3-dependent adhesiveness through multiple integrin classes expressed on T lymphoid progenitors is essential for their homing to the vascularized thymus, while loss of individual integrins either did not or only partially diminish precursor T cell homing (Scimone et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations and citation to Scimone et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Loss of individual integrins either did not or only partially diminish precursor T cell homing.
claims.source: Furthermore, our findings also show that kindlin-3-dependent adhesiveness through multiple integrin classes expressed on T lymphoid progenitors is essential for their homing to the vascularized thymus, while loss of individual integrins either did not or only partially diminish precursor T cell homing (Scimone et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Scimone et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Kindlin-3-deficient T cell progenitors were able to colonize the non-vascularized thymus primordium and develop into SP CD4 and CD8 T cells that are released into the circulation and found in the spleen.
claims.source: Our findings also revealed that kindlin-3-deficient T cell progenitors were able to colonize the non-vascularized thymus primordium and develop into SP CD4 and CD8 T cells that are released into the circulation and found in the spleen.
claims.evidence: Based on observations from fetal thymus colonization studies and Rag2-/- chimera experiments.

claims.claim: Early colonization of the thymus anlage was slightly delayed and less efficient in kindlin-3-deficient embryos.
claims.source: Although early colonization of the thymus anlage was slightly delayed and less efficient, kindlin-3-deficient T cell progenitors were capable to leave the pharyngeal vessels and migrate through the mesenchymal tissue before they reach and enter the thymic anlage.
claims.evidence: Based on immunofluorescence quantification showing reduced but present progenitors in early thymus.

claims.claim: The reduced homing performance of kindlin-3-deficient T cell progenitors was not due to their reduced production in the FL and/or release into the circulation.
claims.source: The reduced homing performance of kindlin-3-deficient T cell progenitors was neither due to their reduced production in the FL and/or release into the circulation, nor due to a defect in sensing chemokine cues that direct them towards the thymic primordium.
claims.evidence: Based on flow cytometry data showing normal numbers of progenitors in FL and their release into circulation.

claims.claim: The reduced homing performance of kindlin-3-deficient T cell progenitors was not due to a defect in sensing chemokine cues.
claims.source: The reduced homing performance of kindlin-3-deficient T cell progenitors was neither due to their reduced production in the FL and/or release into the circulation, nor due to a defect in sensing chemokine cues that direct them towards the thymic primordium.
claims.evidence: Based on thymus attraction assay showing normal chemotaxis of Fermt3-/- progenitors.

claims.claim: Reduced adhesion to the pharyngeal vessel wall accounts for the mild T cell progenitor homing defect of kindlin-3-deficient embryos.
claims.source: So, we assume that reduced adhesion to the pharyngeal vessel wall accounts for the mild T cell progenitor homing defect of kindlin-3-deficient embryos, an assumption, which is also supported by the accumulation of T cell progenitors in the embryonic circulation.
claims.evidence: Based on inference from the observation of progenitor accumulation in fetal blood.

claims.claim: FL-derived T cell progenitors are initially capable but later fail to home to the thymus, suggesting that cell extrinsic rather than cell intrinsic factors are responsible for the impaired colonization.
claims.source: The fact that FL-derived T cell progenitors are initially capable but later fail to home to the thymus suggests that cell extrinsic rather than cell intrinsic factors are responsible for the impaired colonization.
claims.evidence: Based on inference from the temporal pattern of homing defects.

claims.claim: Kindlin-3-deficient thymi exhibited a dramatic drop in the number of DN1 and DN2 cells between E15 to E16, which is the time point when the thymus becomes vascularized.
claims.source: Since kindlin-3-deficient thymi exhibited a dramatic drop in the number of DN1 and DN2 cells between E15 to E16, which is the time point when the thymus becomes vascularized (Liu et al., 2006), we suggest that differences in the adhesive properties of pharyngeal vs. intrathymic vessels account for this phenomenon.
claims.evidence: Based on flow cytometry data and citation to Liu et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Differences in the adhesive properties of pharyngeal vs. intrathymic vessels account for the differential homing capacity of kindlin-3-deficient progenitors.
claims.source: Since kindlin-3-deficient thymi exhibited a dramatic drop in the number of DN1 and DN2 cells between E15 to E16, which is the time point when the thymus becomes vascularized (Liu et al., 2006), we suggest that differences in the adhesive properties of pharyngeal vs. intrathymic vessels account for this phenomenon.
claims.evidence: Based on inference from temporal correlation between vascularization and homing defect.

claims.claim: Kindlin-3-deficient effector T cells can leave the brain vascular system during inflammation when the endothelium expresses ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 at high levels.
claims.source: In support of this hypothesis, we reported that kindlin-3-deficient effector T cells can leave the brain vascular system during inflammation when the endothelium expresses ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 at high levels (Moretti et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Moretti et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Kindlin-3-deficient effector T cells cannot extravasate from inflamed dermal microvessels but are able to leave postcapillary venules of skin-draining inflamed lymph nodes.
claims.source: Similarly, kindlin-3-deficient effector T cells cannot extravasate from inflamed dermal microvessels but are able to leave postcapillary venules of skin-draining inflamed lymph nodes, probably because the high expression of integrin ligands and P-selectin stabilizes the weak adhesions of kindlin-3-deficient T cells (Cohen et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Cohen et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Kindlin-3 is important in stabilizing integrin-ligand interactions by promoting integrin clustering.
claims.source: Beside its role in triggering integrin activation in association with talin-1 (Ma et al., 2008; Montanez et al., 2008; Moser et al., 2009a; Moser et al., 2009b; Moser et al., 2008), kindlin-3 is important in stabilizing integrin-ligand interactions by promoting integrin clustering (Feng et al., 2012; Ye et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Feng et al., 2012 and Ye et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Low shear force conditions may allow adhesion of kindlin-3-deficient T cell progenitors to fetal pharyngeal microvessels, hence enabling their extravasation.
claims.source: Thus, low shear force conditions may allow adhesion of kindlin-3-deficient T cell progenitors to fetal pharyngeal microvessels, hence enabling their extravasation.
claims.evidence: Based on inference from flow chamber experiments and blood flow measurements.

claims.claim: With increasing shear forces at later time points during fetal life, T cell progenitors lacking kindlin-3 are not able to efficiently adhere to and migrate out of microvessels into the thymus.
claims.source: However with increasing shear forces at later time points during fetal life, T cell progenitors lacking kindlin-3 and therefore the ability to strengthening integrin-mediated adhesion are not able to efficiently adhere to and migrate out of microvessels into the thymus.
claims.evidence: Based on inference from flow chamber experiments showing detachment at high shear and blood flow measurements showing increasing shear during development.

claims.claim: High expression of α4β1 on the surface of FL-derived T cell progenitors supports the ability to resist low shear forces.
claims.source: The ability to resist low shear forces is also supported by an early report that found high expression of α4β1 on the surface of FL-derived T cell progenitors (Kawakami et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Kawakami et al., 1999.

claims.claim: α4β1-mediated adhesiveness to VCAM-1 is less affected by loss of kindlin-3 in contrast to αLβ2 integrin-mediated adhesion to ICAM-1.
claims.source: In addition, we and others have shown that α4β1-mediated adhesiveness to VCAM-1 is less affected by loss of kindlin-3 in contrast to αLβ2 integrin-mediated adhesion to ICAM-1 (Klapproth et al., 2015; Manevich-Mendelson et al., 2009; Moretti et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Klapproth et al., 2015; Manevich-Mendelson et al., 2009; Moretti et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Lack of β1 integrin expression on hematopoietic stem cells abolishes their extravasation and homing to the BM.
claims.source: In this respect, it is interesting to note that lack of β1 integrin expression on hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) abolishes their extravasation and homing to the BM (Potocnik et al., 2000)
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Potocnik et al., 2000.

claims.claim: Kindlin-3-deficient HSCs revealed significantly diminished but not absent homing to the BM.
claims.source: In this respect, it is interesting to note that lack of β1 integrin expression on hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) abolishes their extravasation and homing to the BM (Potocnik et al., 2000), whereas kindlin-3-deficient HSCs revealed significantly diminished but not absent homing to the BM (Ruppert et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Ruppert et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Kindlin-3 is dispensable for integrin-mediated T cell adhesion and signalling at low and indispensable at high vascular shear forces.
claims.source: Taken together, our work demonstrates that kindlin-3 is dispensable for integrin-mediated T cell adhesion and signalling at low and indispensable at high vascular shear forces.
claims.evidence: Based on synthesis of multiple experimental observations including flow chamber assays, blood flow measurements, and in vivo adhesion studies.

claims.claim: This work shows a general, crucial role of integrins during T cell development.
claims.source: Furthermore, we also show a general, crucial role of integrins during T cell development and suggest an additional not yet investigated T cell phenotype in LADIII patients.
claims.evidence: Based on inference from the comprehensive analysis of integrin function via kindlin-3 deficiency.

claims.claim: There may be an additional not yet investigated T cell phenotype in LADIII patients.
claims.source: Furthermore, we also show a general, crucial role of integrins during T cell development and suggest an additional not yet investigated T cell phenotype in LADIII patients.
claims.evidence: Based on speculation from the findings in mouse models.

claims.claim: Loss of kindlin-3 impairs the functions of all integrins on hematopoietic cells studied so far.
claims.source: Consequently, loss of kindlin-3 impairs the functions of all integrins on hematopoietic cells studied so far and leads to severe defects affecting platelets, leukocytes, osteoclasts and hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) (Krüger et al., 2008; Moser et al., 2009a; Moser et al., 2008; Ruppert et al., 2015; Schmidt et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies (Krüger et al., 2008; Moser et al., 2009a; Moser et al., 2008; Ruppert et al., 2015; Schmidt et al., 2011).

claims.claim: Loss-of-function mutations in the human KINDLIN-3/FERMT3 gene cause leukocyte adhesion deficiency type-III (LAD-III) syndrome.
claims.source: In line with genetic studies in mice, loss-of-function mutations in the human KINDLIN-3/FERMT3 gene cause leukocyte adhesion deficiency type-III (LAD-III) syndrome, which is characterized by severe bleedings, infections and accumulation of HSPCs in the blood circulation (Kuijpers et al., 2009; Malinin et al., 2009; Mory et al., 2008; Ruppert et al., 2015; Svensson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies (Kuijpers et al., 2009; Malinin et al., 2009; Mory et al., 2008; Ruppert et al., 2015; Svensson et al., 2009).

claims.claim: LAD-III syndrome is characterized by severe bleedings, infections and accumulation of HSPCs in the blood circulation.
claims.source: In line with genetic studies in mice, loss-of-function mutations in the human KINDLIN-3/FERMT3 gene cause leukocyte adhesion deficiency type-III (LAD-III) syndrome, which is characterized by severe bleedings, infections and accumulation of HSPCs in the blood circulation (Kuijpers et al., 2009; Malinin et al., 2009; Mory et al., 2008; Ruppert et al., 2015; Svensson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to clinical studies (Kuijpers et al., 2009; Malinin et al., 2009; Mory et al., 2008; Ruppert et al., 2015; Svensson et al., 2009).

results.result: Loss of kindlin-3 leads to progressive thymus atrophy after postnatal day 3, with significantly reduced cellularity at all time points analyzed, despite normal morphology until P3. No compensatory expression of kindlin-1 or kindlin-2 was observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C8 collectively demonstrate progressive thymus atrophy in Fermt3-/- mice with strong supporting data from morphological images (C3, C4), quantitative cellularity measurements (C5-C7), and Western blot analysis excluding compensation (C8). The temporal progression and statistical significance are well-documented.

results.result: Fermt3-/- thymi display normal thymic architecture and T cell differentiation at P3, but show progressive architectural changes and altered T cell subset distribution by P6, with reduced DN cells at both time points. Normal expression of TCR and costimulatory molecules suggests intrathymic differentiation proceeds independently of kindlin-3.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C16 are well-supported by immunofluorescence (C9), histology (C10), and flow cytometry data (C11-C14, C16). The inference that differentiation is kindlin-3-independent (C15) is reasonable given normal relative SP numbers at P3 and normal surface marker expression, though the conclusion could be strengthened with additional functional assays.

results.result: Thymus atrophy in Fermt3-/- mice is caused by reduced thymocyte proliferation rather than increased apoptosis. Kindlin-3-deficient T cells can form immune synapses with normal molecular recruitment but show impaired proliferation under weak stimulation conditions, indicating defective integrin-mediated contact with APCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C25 provide strong evidence through multiple complementary approaches: apoptosis assays (C17-C18), BrdU incorporation (C19-C20), immune synapse analysis (C21-C22), and in vitro proliferation assays (C23-C24). The mechanistic conclusion (C25) is well-supported by the observation that proliferation is normal under strong but not weak stimulation.

results.result: Fermt3-/- mice show severely reduced DN1 and DN2 thymocytes and accumulation of hematopoietic progenitors in blood circulation, suggesting impaired T cell progenitor homing to the thymus.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C30 are supported by flow cytometry data showing reduced DN populations (C27-C28) and increased circulating progenitors (C29). The inference of impaired extravasation (C30) is reasonable given the accumulation in blood, though direct visualization of extravasation would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Transfer of Fermt3-/- fetal liver cells fails to reconstitute T cell development in Rag2-/- recipients, with almost no DN1-2 cells detected. However, a small number of progenitors can enter the thymus, differentiate into mature T cells, and populate the spleen, indicating kindlin-3 is critical for homing but not for intrathymic differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C35 are well-supported by chimera experiments with flow cytometry data (C31-C34). The conclusion (C35) that kindlin-3 is important for homing but not differentiation is justified by the observation that the few progenitors that enter can complete development, though the small numbers limit statistical power.

results.result: The T cell progenitor homing defect in kindlin-3 deficiency is of hematopoietic origin, as demonstrated by conditional deletion experiments, competitive chimeras showing disproportionate representation of Fermt3-/- cells, and kindlin-3-EGFP expression restricted to CD45+ leukocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40 provide strong evidence through multiple complementary approaches: conditional deletion (C36), competitive chimeras (C37-C38), and cell-type specific expression analysis (C39). The conclusion (C40) is well-justified by the convergent evidence from these independent experimental approaches.

results.result: Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors can colonize the early thymus primordium at E11.5-E13.5, albeit at lower numbers than WT, and develop into DN1-2 cells. However, a dramatic drop in DN1-2 cells occurs at E15-16.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44 are supported by immunofluorescence quantification (C41-C43) and flow cytometry (C44) showing temporal progression of the homing defect. The data clearly demonstrate that early colonization is possible but becomes severely impaired at later embryonic stages, correlating with thymus vascularization.

results.result: T cell progenitor development and release from fetal liver is normal in Fermt3-/- embryos, with comparable absolute numbers but increased frequency due to reduced FL cellularity. However, progenitors accumulate in fetal circulation between E12 and E13.5, indicating impaired extravasation.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 are well-supported by flow cytometry data showing normal progenitor numbers in FL (C45-C46) and differential kinetics in circulation (C47-C48). The data effectively rule out defects in progenitor generation and point to extravasation as the primary defect.

results.result: Fermt3-/- T cell progenitors can sense chemokine gradients and migrate toward thymic lobes in vitro, and can develop normally into mature T cells in fetal thymus organ culture, indicating that chemotaxis and intrathymic differentiation are kindlin-3-independent.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 are supported by time-lapse microscopy (C49) and FTOC experiments (C50). The conclusion (C51) that multiple steps of T cell development are kindlin-3-independent is well-justified, though the in vitro nature of these assays may not fully recapitulate in vivo conditions.

results.result: The differential homing capacity of Fermt3-/- progenitors to early versus late thymus is not explained by differences in kindlin-3/talin-1 protein levels, integrin surface expression, vascular network formation, or adhesion molecule expression on vessels.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C55 systematically rule out multiple potential explanations through Western blot (C52), flow cytometry (C53), and immunofluorescence (C54-C55). This negative data is important for narrowing down the mechanism, though one citation (C54) relies on unpublished data which weakens the claim slightly.

results.result: Blood flow velocity and shear rates increase during embryonic development (E12.5 to E16.5). T cell progenitors preferentially adhere to VCAM-1 rather than ICAM-1 under flow conditions, and Fermt3-/- progenitors show significantly reduced shear force resistance on VCAM-1, suggesting that increasing shear forces during development prevent Fermt3-/- progenitor adhesion.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C60 provide strong mechanistic insight through intravital microscopy (C56) and flow chamber assays (C57-C59). The inference (C60) that increasing shear forces explain the temporal homing defect is well-supported by the convergent evidence, representing a key mechanistic finding.

results.result: Fermt3 hypomorphic T cells show reduced adhesion in lymph node vasculature and preferentially adhere in vessel segments with lower blood flow velocity and shear rates compared to WT cells, demonstrating that kindlin-3 is crucial for stabilizing integrin-mediated adhesion under high vascular shear forces.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63 provide strong in vivo validation through intravital microscopy showing differential adhesion patterns based on local shear rates. This elegant experiment directly demonstrates the shear-dependent function of kindlin-3 in a physiological setting, strongly supporting the proposed mechanism.

results.result: In the absence of kindlin-3, normal thymus architecture is initially formed with proper spatial organization of T cell subsets, indicating that chemokine-driven migration and positioning within the 3D thymic environment does not require kindlin-3-mediated integrin activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 are supported by histological and immunofluorescence observations showing normal thymic architecture. The inference (C65-C66) that intrathymic migration is kindlin-3-independent is reasonable and consistent with prior literature (Lämmermann et al., 2008), though direct migration assays within thymic tissue would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Thymus atrophy in kindlin-3-deficient mice has two main causes: reduced thymocyte proliferation due to weakened APC interactions, and a severe T cell progenitor homing defect that becomes apparent at the end of embryogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C70 synthesize the major findings with support from proliferation data (C68) and developmental timing analysis (C70). The citation to similar findings in LFA-1 and talin-1 knockouts (C69) provides additional support. This represents a well-supported summary of the two main mechanisms.

results.result: T cell progenitors colonize the initially avascular thymus anlage starting at E11.5. Kindlin-3-deficient progenitors can colonize the non-vascularized thymus primordium, though with slight delay and reduced efficiency, and develop into mature T cells. Kindlin-3-dependent adhesiveness through multiple integrin classes is essential for homing to the vascularized thymus.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C78 integrate established knowledge (C71-C72) with experimental findings showing differential requirements for kindlin-3 in early versus late thymus colonization. The conclusion (C75) about multiple integrin classes is supported by comparison to single integrin knockouts (C76), providing important mechanistic insight.

results.result: The reduced homing of kindlin-3-deficient progenitors is not due to defects in progenitor production, release, or chemokine sensing, but rather to reduced adhesion to vessel walls. The temporal pattern suggests cell-extrinsic factors are responsible, with the dramatic drop in DN1-2 cells at E15-16 coinciding with thymus vascularization, implicating differences in adhesive properties between pharyngeal and intrathymic vessels.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C84 provide logical reasoning supported by experimental data ruling out alternative mechanisms (C79-C80) and temporal correlation with vascularization (C83). The inference about vessel differences (C84) is reasonable given the timing, though direct comparison of adhesive properties would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Kindlin-3-deficient T cells can extravasate from inflamed brain vessels and lymph node postcapillary venules expressing high levels of adhesion molecules, but not from inflamed dermal microvessels. Kindlin-3 stabilizes integrin-ligand interactions by promoting integrin clustering.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87 are supported by citations to prior publications (Moretti et al., 2013; Cohen et al., 2013; Feng et al., 2012; Ye et al., 2013). This provides important context for understanding how high adhesion molecule expression can partially compensate for kindlin-3 deficiency, supporting the proposed mechanism.

results.result: Low shear force conditions allow adhesion of kindlin-3-deficient progenitors to fetal pharyngeal vessels, but increasing shear forces at later developmental stages prevent efficient adhesion and extravasation. High α4β1 expression on FL-derived progenitors and its relative resistance to kindlin-3 loss support this model.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C91 synthesize the mechanistic model with support from flow chamber data and literature citations (Kawakami et al., 1999; Klapproth et al., 2015). The model is internally consistent and well-supported by the experimental evidence, though the inference nature of C88-C89 should be noted.

results.result: Comparison with β1 integrin knockout HSCs (which show complete loss of BM homing) versus kindlin-3-deficient HSCs (which show reduced but not absent homing) suggests kindlin-3 deficiency allows some residual integrin function.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 are supported by citations to prior publications (Potocnik et al., 2000; Ruppert et al., 2015). This comparison provides important context for understanding the partial versus complete loss-of-function phenotypes, supporting the model that kindlin-3 enhances but is not absolutely required for integrin function under certain conditions.

results.result: Kindlin-3 is dispensable for integrin-mediated T cell adhesion and signaling at low shear forces but indispensable at high shear forces. This work demonstrates a general, crucial role of integrins during T cell development and suggests potential T cell phenotypes in LAD-III patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 represent well-supported major conclusions synthesizing the experimental findings. However, C96 is speculative about human patients and lacks direct evidence. The overall conclusion (C94) is strongly supported by the comprehensive experimental data, though the clinical speculation (C96) is appropriately tentative.

results.result: Loss of kindlin-3 impairs all integrin functions on hematopoietic cells studied, affecting platelets, leukocytes, osteoclasts, and HSPCs. In humans, KINDLIN-3/FERMT3 mutations cause LAD-III syndrome characterized by severe bleeding, infections, and HSPC accumulation in blood.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99 are well-supported by multiple citations to prior publications establishing the broad role of kindlin-3 in hematopoietic cells and the clinical phenotype of LAD-III syndrome. This provides important background context for the current study.
